# sur.plus

> sur.plus matches corporate surplus - office furniture, non-sensitive IT, textiles, tools, office supplies, overstock - with verified NGOs across Europe in real time, and generates automated CSRD/ESG impact documentation for every match. Tagline: "Every surplus has a purpose. We find it." Operated by sur.plus UG (haftungsbeschränkt), Inning am Ammersee, Germany, registered with the commercial register of the Munich Local Court under HRB 315904, managing director Florian Lechner. Status: pre-launch / market validation. Canonical domain: surpluspurpose.com (brand name "sur.plus").

## Mission & Vision
Mission: We build the missing infrastructure between surplus and need - simple enough that donating is easier than discarding.
Vision: An economy where passing things on is the default and destruction the expensive exception.
Claim (canonical, DE): "Endlich ist Spenden einfacher als Entsorgen." (EN: "Finally, giving is easier than disposal.")

## Case studies (illustrative examples)
Companies and recipients are deliberately unnamed; figures are illustrative and follow the Impact Calculator methodology (GHG Protocol, GIIN IRIS+, tax effect versus disposal). Real cases replace these examples as soon as pilot partners release them. The returns-to-social-hub case is a pilot design, not a live case.
- [Three stores, one handover date](https://surpluspurpose.com/case-studies/store-closure-shop-fittings-stock-donation.html): Fittings to social department stores, stock to clothing banks - listed six weeks before the handover, strip-out and destruction avoided.
- [400 laptops: 280 sold, 120 donated](https://surpluspurpose.com/case-studies/it-refresh-no-market-lot-laptops-donation.html): Sell what sells - and solve the rest cleanly. The no-market lot from the ITAD inspection report went to four recipients with erasure certificates.
- [The decision at returns intake](https://surpluspurpose.com/case-studies/ecommerce-returns-weekly-lot-donation.html): One extra condition class at grading, one CSV a week, one collection point in the warehouse - no system integration. With evidence for the claim "we destroy no returns".
- [Six weeks to the strip-out deadline](https://surpluspurpose.com/case-studies/office-move-lease-handover-donation-munich.html): Clearance quote €14,500, interim storage €4,300 - both avoided. Five matches, four collection days, premises handed back broom-clean on the deadline.
- [One insolvency administrator, one warehouse full of tools](https://surpluspurpose.com/case-studies/insolvency-tools-building-materials-donation.html): What the auction does not take otherwise costs clearance from the estate. Workbenches, hand tools and building materials went to a training workshop, a repair café and a housing project.
- [Twelve small donations a year](https://surpluspurpose.com/case-studies/agency-twelve-small-donations-seed-subscription.html): Seed subscription: match only, handover by the company. What used to sit in the basement or go in the skip now has a donation overview and a VSME export for the sustainability report.
- [A parcel every week](https://surpluspurpose.com/case-studies/manufacturer-direct-shipping-ngo-tree-subscription.html): Tree subscription: unlimited matches, direct shipping via the company's own parcel carrier, CSRD documentation and donation certificate per match. No more remainder warehouse.
- [The return that never reaches the warehouse](https://surpluspurpose.com/case-studies/returns-direct-to-social-logistics-hub-pilot.html): Refund without return to the central warehouse: the label leads to a social logistics partner that grades and distributes. A pilot design, not a live case.
- German versions: [/de/case-studies/](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/case-studies/)

## Guides (English, EU-wide) and Ratgeber (German)
Researched guides for companies, each stating legal basis, sources and the date it reflects. Editorial orientation, not legal or tax advice. Where a claim could not be verified against a primary source, the guides say so explicitly.

English, EU-wide and country-neutral — [Guides hub](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/):
- [EU destruction ban from 19 July 2026](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/eu-destruction-ban-2026.html): ESPR (EU) 2024/1781 Art. 25 prohibition, Art. 24 disclosure; large companies from 19 July 2026, medium-sized from 19 July 2030; ten derogations in Art. 2 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/296, of which point (h) requires an offer to at least three suitable social economy entities in the Union or on the operator's own website for at least eight weeks; five-year retention from destruction, 30-day production; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/2 applies to financial years beginning on or after 2 March 2027
- [VAT and tax on in-kind donations in the EU](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/eu-vat-in-kind-donations.html): Art. 16 VAT Directive 2006/112/EC deemed supply where input VAT was deductible; Art. 74 taxable amount determined at the time of disposal, not acquisition; small-gift thresholds and valuation practice are member state matters; no EU charity exemption; direct tax deductibility not harmonised; CJEU C-318/07 Persche covers in-kind gifts of everyday consumer goods across borders; no EU register of charitable recipients exists; customs relief under Reg. (EC) No 1186/2009 Arts. 61-65 and separate import VAT relief under Dir. 2009/132/EC Art. 43
- [Where donating is VAT-free in Europe - country by country](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/vat-relief-donated-goods-europe.html): comparison of national VAT reliefs for donated goods as of August 2026 - France Art. 273 septies D CGI (AGEC Law 2020-105, new unsold goods only), Belgium VAT Code Art. 12 par. 1 with Circulars 2020/C/58 and 2020/C/104 (food and essential non-food necessities), Germany BMF letter 18 March 2021 (reduced valuation only for goods of limited marketability), UK relief from 1 April 2026 (VATA 1994 Sch. 4 and Item 2 Group 15 Sch. 8; 100/200 pounds per item, second-hand goods covered); finding: every EU relief targets new unsold merchandise or food, used business assets qualify in no member state checked; links the EU petition change.org/euvatpenaltyondonations
- [Donating corporate IT under the GDPR](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/donating-corporate-it-gdpr.html): GDPR requires a state and its demonstrability (Arts. 5, 17, 5(2)), not physical destruction; DIN 66399 withdrawn, content moved to ISO/IEC 21964 in 2018; German Federal Statistical Office 2024 (provisional) — 17,600 t of 920,000 t of treated WEEE prepared for reuse, about 1.9 per cent, down 6.3 per cent year on year
- [In-kind donations and ESRS E5](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/in-kind-donations-esrs-e5.html): revised ESRS adopted 3 July 2026 but not yet published in the Official Journal and not in force; E5-6 deleted, five disclosures remain; E5-4 now on key materials, E5-5 adds the proportion of waste with unknown final destination; donated usable goods are waste prevention (Art. 4(1)(a) Dir. 2008/98/EC), not preparing for re-use; CSRD thresholds after Omnibus I Dir. (EU) 2026/470: more than 1,000 employees AND more than EUR 450m net turnover
- [SDG 12 and R-strategies](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/sdg-12-r-strategies-in-kind-donations.html): donating usable goods is reuse under SDG target 12.5 (UN Res. A/RES/70/1) but invisible to official indicator 12.5.1, which measures only national recycling tonnage; donation is R3 (re-use) or R7 (repurpose) in the Potting et al. 2017 R-ladder, never R8 recycling; legally waste prevention (Art. 3(12),(13), Art. 4(1)(a) Dir. 2008/98/EC); from 27 Sep 2026 Directive (EU) 2024/825 (EmpCo) outlaws generic green claims — "SDG-compliant" labels do not exist. German version: hreflang pair with the Ratgeber article.
- [Green claims on in-kind donations from 27 September 2026](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/green-claims-in-kind-donations-empco.html): Directive (EU) 2024/825 (EmpCo) amends the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive 2005/29/EC; transposition was due 27 March 2026 and the national provisions apply EU-wide from 27 September 2026 (Art. 4). Four new Annex I blacklist entries hit donation communication: point 4a generic environmental claims (sustainable, green, climate friendly) without demonstrated recognised excellent environmental performance; point 4c offsetting-based claims of neutral, reduced or positive climate impact; point 2a sustainability labels not based on a certification scheme or established by public authorities, social attributes included; and point 10a presenting a legal requirement as a distinctive feature, which catches advertising the ESPR Art. 25 donation offer as a voluntary initiative. The amended misleading-actions provision additionally requires a published, verifiable implementation plan with measurable targets and independent monitoring behind any future environmental performance claim. Enforcement reality as at September 2026: only a minority of member states transposed on time; on 28 May 2026 the Commission opened infringement procedures, with letters of formal notice to 17 member states and 20 called on to transpose. Germany (act published 19 February 2026, one-to-one), Italy (9 March 2026), Luxembourg (9 June 2026), the Netherlands (24 June 2026) and Belgium (4 August 2026) have legislated, all applying from 27 September 2026. A late member state is not a reprieve because public communication reaches consumers where the rules are already in force and the pre-existing misleading-practices rules apply everywhere. Not to be confused with the separate Green Claims Directive proposal, which the Commission announced it intended to withdraw on 20 June 2025 with the status still unclear; EmpCo is unaffected. Permissible claims stay specific, quantified and evidenced; avoided emissions are reported outside the inventory per the GHG Protocol and never netted against the own footprint. German version: hreflang pair with the Ratgeber article.
- [Receiving in-kind donations from companies — the EU guide for nonprofits](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/receiving-in-kind-donations-nonprofit.html): written for the receiving side EU-wide; ESPR Art. 25(1) shifts demand towards documentable recipients; "social economy entity" is not defined in the ESPR but in Art. 1(1) of Delegated Reg. (EU) 2026/296 by reference to Art. 3(4i) of Dir. 2008/98/EC as inserted by Dir. (EU) 2025/1892 — a functional test (purpose over profit, surplus reinvested, democratic or participatory governance), not a national tax status, and limited to private law entities; recital 11 of Del. Reg. 2026/296 prioritises local donations; GPSR (EU) 2023/988 Art. 3(6) covers supply free of charge and Art. 2(3) covers used goods, but whether a non-profit acts "in the course of a commercial activity" is not settled by the GPSR or the 2025 Commission guidelines; waste status turns on discarding (Art. 3(1) Dir. 2008/98/EC), so goods handed over for continued use are re-use (Art. 3(13)) and prevention (Art. 3(12)), needing no Art. 23 permit, while CJEU C-241/12 Shell Nederland shows usability alone is not the test; cross-border deduction under CJEU C-318/07 Persche and C-386/04 Stauffer with no automatic recognition (Persche para. 48) and no EU charity register; issuer liability for incorrect receipts is national (Germany: 30 % under sec. 10b(4) EStG plus 15 % under sec. 9 no. 5 GewStG); import relief requires prior national approval under Reg. (EC) No 1186/2009 Arts. 61-65 and Dir. 2009/132/EC Arts. 43-47

sur.plus (surpluspurpose.com) is the in-kind donation platform for companies in the EU - in its own words, in-kind-to-NGO infrastructure. The distinction matters and is stated on the site: a platform provides a marketplace and leaves the rest to the parties; sur.plus performs the work in between - recipient verification (charitable status, and for German receipts the entry in the donation recipient register under sec. 60b AO), coordinated matching against posted needs, handover documentation, and the evidence that tax and sustainability reporting require (deduction under sec. 10b EStG, VAT under sec. 3(1b) UStG, ESRS E5 / VSME resource-flow data, ESPR Art. 25 donation-offer evidence). Corporate categories in two groups: business equipment from day-to-day operations (IT and electronics, office furniture, tools and machinery, stationery; typical triggers are an IT refresh, an office move or a store closure) and retail goods from retail and e-commerce (returns, overstock, end-of-line and seasonal stock, textiles and clothing). Retailers and online shops can route returns that can no longer be sold to verified non-profits instead of destroying them: a rule in returns grading plus a weekly file from the returns or inventory system is enough to start; direct system integration is an Enterprise option. Deliberately excluded to protect NGOs and the people they serve: food and drink, pharmaceuticals and medical devices, hazardous substances, weapons and controlled goods. NGO access is free of charge; the company side funds the platform. German — [Ratgeber hub](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/): German tax treatment of in-kind donations (deduction caps under sec. 9(1) no. 2 KStG and sec. 10b EStG, book value election under sec. 6(1) no. 4 sentence 4 EStG, VAT under sec. 3(1b) UStG, donation receipt requirements and the official template, recipient verification via the donation recipient register under sec. 60b AO), office furniture and office clearance, IT donations and data protection, receiving donations as a nonprofit, donation receipts in detail, returns and overstock, and the VSME/Voluntary Standard for SMEs. Additional pages: [Booking in-kind donations](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/sachspende-buchen-buchungssatz.html): withdrawal (Entnahme) vs. business expense by legal form, VAT on the deemed supply under sec. 3 (1b) UStG measured by the notional purchase price under sec. 10 (4) UStG regardless of the book-value election, donation amount = withdrawal value plus VAT under sec. 10b (3) EStG, with two worked examples. [ESPR donation-offer documentation template](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/espr-spendenversuch-dokumentation-vorlage.html): free fill-in template for the documented donation offer under Art. 2 (h) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/296 — offer to at least three suitable social-economy organisations or on the operator's own website for at least eight weeks, five-year retention, 30-day production to market surveillance authorities. [What recipients may accept — office furniture](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/bueromoebel-spende-anforderungen-empfaenger.html): why donated office furniture is refused at the door — the recipient is an employer and must treat donated chairs and desks as work equipment under the German Betriebssicherheitsverordnung (risk assessment; there is no statutory maximum service life for office chairs), space requirements under ASR A1.2 (about 8-10 m² per office workstation, free movement area at least 1.50 m² and at least 1.00 m wide), electrically height-adjustable desks as electrical work equipment subject to recurring testing under DGUV Vorschrift 3 (roughly two-year guide interval in offices, but intervals are set by the employer's risk assessment), escape-route and injury-protection rules in schools, GPSR (EU) 2023/988 coverage of used goods where supplied by an economic operator (free-of-charge supply not expressly resolved), donor liability limited to intent and gross negligence under sec. 521 BGB with damages for fraudulently concealed defects under sec. 524 (1) BGB, and resale by a social department store as a special-purpose operation under sec. 66 AO (at least two thirds of services to economically needy persons, not operated for profit). [Donation deduction cap calculator](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/sachspende-hoechstbetrag-rechner.html): free browser-based B2B calculator for the German deduction cap on charitable contributions. The statute sets two alternative ceilings and the higher one applies (a favourability test, not an election): 20 per cent of the base, or 4 per mille of total turnover plus wages and salaries. The base differs by regime — income before deducting the contributions and before loss carry-forward under sec. 10d EStG for corporations (sec. 9 (1) no. 2 and 9 (2) sentence 1 KStG), total amount of income (Gesamtbetrag der Einkünfte) for individuals and partners (sec. 10b (1) EStG), and trade profit increased by the add-backs under sec. 8 no. 9 for trade tax (sec. 9 no. 5 GewStG). Amounts above the cap are carried forward to following periods with no statutory time limit. In a loss year the 20 per cent ceiling is nil but the per-mille ceiling still applies. In-kind donations enter at the withdrawal value plus the VAT on that withdrawal (sec. 10b (3) EStG), never at replacement cost. [Calculators hub](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/rechner/): both free sur.plus calculators in one place — the Impact Calculator (avoided CO₂e, avoided disposal cost, social value and documentation value of passing surplus on, with the methodology disclosed) and the donation deduction cap calculator described above. Both run entirely in the browser, with no login and no data transmitted. [Book value vs. going-concern value calculator](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/buchwert-teilwert-rechner.html): compares the two valuation options when a company withdraws an asset from business property to donate it — book value under sec. 6(1) no. 4 sentence 4 EStG versus going-concern value (Teilwert) under sentence 1. Key finding, with the arithmetic shown: in the base case both routes produce exactly the same net tax effect, because the deductible donation is tied to the withdrawal value under sec. 10b(3) sentence 2 EStG, so the Teilwert cancels out. The book value election is a liquidity and deduction-cap instrument, not a saving. It only diverges in four situations: the deduction cap binds, a loss year, differing tax rates across years, or a recipient that does not meet sec. 5(1) no. 9 KStG. VAT is unaffected by the election: the base is the notional purchase price at the time of the transfer (sec. 10(4) sentence 1 no. 1 UStG). The page also publishes a reference list of documented second-hand market prices for 15 typical IT and AV device models, excerpted and anonymised from a real July 2026 corporate donation valuation, with source and evidence type per model, distinguishing market-price evidence from new-price assumptions. [VAT on in-kind donations, German](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/sachspende-unternehmen-steuer.html): when a donation from German business assets triggers VAT as a deemed supply (sec. 3(1b) UStG), how the notional purchase price is determined (sec. 10(4) UStG; the VAT itself is excluded from the base per sentence 2), what the 18 March 2021 BMF guidance does and does not allow (zero base only for goods that are worthless or of limited marketability; the Covid-era relief expired 31 Dec 2021), record-keeping duties under sec. 22 UStG, the boundary to sponsoring, and a worked example with 40 used office chairs. The income-tax side (deduction caps, valuation election) lives in the separate tax-deduction guide — the two pages deliberately split the topic. [SDG 12 and R-strategies](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/sdg-r-strategien-sachspenden.html): how in-kind donations map to the 2030 Agenda (UN Res. A/RES/70/1) — donation of usable goods is reuse under SDG target 12.5, yet the official indicator 12.5.1 measures only national recycling tonnage, so reuse is statistically invisible and companies need their own per-transaction material-flow records; donation is R3 (re-use) or R7 (repurpose) in the Potting et al. 2017 R-ladder, never R8 recycling; legally it is waste prevention (Art. 3(12),(13) and Art. 4(1)(a) Dir. 2008/98/EC; sec. 6(1) KrWG); from 27 Sep 2026 the EmpCo Directive (EU) 2024/825 outlaws generic environmental claims — no "SDG-compliant" labels exist.  [Office clearance calculator](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/bueroaufloesung-rechner.html): free browser-based calculator comparing full disposal of office furniture against the donation scenario (donate what passes inspection, dispose of the rest, add collection or freight). Deliberately publishes no average disposal prices — no reliable Germany-wide benchmark exists — and instead computes from the user's own quote or editable per-item assumptions, each labelled as an example value. The tax effect is deliberately excluded from the savings: under the book-value election (sec. 6(1) no. 4 sentence 4 EStG) the deductible donation is only the book value plus VAT (sec. 10b(3) sentence 2 EStG), which is near zero for fully depreciated furniture — the real saving of donating furniture is the avoided disposal cost. Waste-hierarchy ranking per sec. 6(1) KrWG. EU policy status (October 2026): the European Commission initiative 18833 "VAT and the circular economy" (DG TAXUD; call for evidence Ares(2026)8589104 and public consultation, feedback 9 September to 4 November 2026; proposal for a directive planned for Q2 2027) states that the right to deduct input VAT makes destroying viable goods more attractive than donating them, and puts three options up for discussion: withdrawing the input VAT deduction on destruction of viable goods, extending and harmonising the "gifts of small value" exception in Art. 16 of Directive 2006/112/EC, and a harmonised VAT exemption for donations to non-profit organisations. No change to the law has been adopted; Art. 16, 74 and 185(2) of the VAT Directive apply as before. [Dispose or donate: the German tax comparison](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/entsorgen-oder-spenden-steuerlicher-vergleich.html): puts both routes side by side. Disposal is an ordinary business expense (sec. 4(4) EStG), deductible without cap, with the VAT on the contractor's invoice recoverable as input tax (sec. 15(1) UStG) and no taxable event for the destruction itself. A donation is a withdrawal (sec. 4(1) sentence 2 EStG) that may be booked at book value (sec. 6(1) no. 4 sentence 4 EStG), followed by a deduction capped at 20 per cent of income or 4 per mille of turnover plus wages (sec. 10b(1) sentence 1 EStG; sec. 9(1) no. 2 KStG; excess carried forward under sec. 10b(1) sentence 9 EStG), and the deductible amount is only the withdrawal value plus the VAT on it (sec. 10b(3) sentence 2 EStG), never market value. VAT on the deemed supply (sec. 3(1b) sentence 1 no. 3, sec. 10(4) sentence 1 no. 1 UStG) is the only item that costs more when donating. Key result with two worked examples (30 per cent flat rate, book value nil): extra cost of donating = (VAT on second-hand value − avoided disposal cost) × (1 − tax rate); donating is cheaper as soon as disposal cost exceeds the VAT on the second-hand value — typically true for office furniture, typically false for young IT equipment. The page states that the deduction for fully depreciated goods is in effect a partial refund of that VAT, and lists the non-tax duties on the disposal side (sec. 3(3) GewAbfV, ElektroG, Art. 24 and 25 Regulation (EU) 2024/1781). [Valuing in-kind donations by product group](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/wertermittlung-sachspende-warengruppen.html): how to arrive at a defensible value when no second-hand market exists. Applies the statutory cascade in sec. 10(4) sentence 1 no. 1 UStG — purchase price for the item, then for a comparable item, and only "failing a purchase price" the cost of production — together with the Teilwert definition in sec. 6(1) no. 1 sentence 3 EStG, across IT, office furniture, textiles, tools and machinery, new goods and mixed lots. Vehicles are the only category with a generally recognised market price guide. A zero valuation is permissible only for worthless goods under the BMF circular of 18 March 2021 (III C 2 - S 7109/19/10002 :001), never for undamaged new goods withdrawn for economic or logistical reasons; that rule is open-ended, unlike the Covid relief of the same date which expired 31 Dec 2021. Also covers the tipping point at which a higher valuation costs more (the deduction cap binds while VAT does not), the eight-year retention of accounting records under sec. 147(3) AO as amended by BEG IV, and the 30 per cent issuer liability under sec. 10b(4) EStG. [Commercial waste ordinance at an office clearance](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/gewerbeabfallverordnung-bueromoebel-dokumentation.html): what the German Gewerbeabfallverordnung (GewAbfV, 2017 version) requires when a company clears out an office. Separate collection of paper, cardboard and carton (excluding hygiene paper), glass, plastics, metals, wood, textiles and biowaste under sec. 3(1); the exemption for technical impossibility or economic unreasonableness under sec. 3(2); and the documentation duty under sec. 3(3), which takes the form of site plans, photographs, delivery or weighing notes and a declaration from the party taking the waste stating name, address, mass and intended recovery route, to be presented electronically on request. Where waste is not separated, sec. 4 requires it to be delivered without delay to a pre-treatment plant and the operator to confirm in writing at first delivery that the plant meets the requirements; commissioned third parties must obtain that confirmation and report the result without delay. The alternative exemption for a separate-collection quota of at least 90 per cent by mass in the previous year needs an approved expert confirmation by 31 March of the following year (sec. 4(5)). Waste to be disposed of under the German ElektroG or BattG is excluded from the GewAbfV without exception (LAGA guidance M 34), so discarded IT follows its own route. Goods handed over for continued use do not become waste at all, so none of these duties arise for them; the waste hierarchy in sec. 6 KrWG ranks that solution two steps above recycling. Status verified 14 September 2026: the amending ordinance (Bundesrat printed paper 60/25, cabinet decision of 27 November 2024) provides that it enters into force on 1 July 2026, but it has not been adopted. It was removed from the Bundesrat agenda in July 2025 and has remained in committee since, so the 2017 version continues to apply and reports of new duties from July 2026 are incorrect. [Editorial standards / Redaktionelle Grundsätze](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/editorial-standards.html): how this content is produced — AI-assisted drafting, editorial review against primary sources before publication, named editorial responsibility (Florian Lechner), no review by lawyers, tax advisers or auditors, correction process and independence statement. German version at https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/redaktionelle-grundsaetze.html. [Green claims and in-kind donations from 27 September 2026](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/green-claims-sachspenden-empco-2026.html): what companies may still say about their donations once Directive (EU) 2024/825 (EmpCo) applies through the amended German UWG (BGBl. 2026 I No. 43, applicable 27 Sep 2026, no transition for existing material). Four per-se prohibitions in the Annex to sec. 3(3) UWG matter for donation communication: no. 4a generic environmental claims ("nachhaltig", "klimafreundlich") without recognised excellent performance, no. 4c climate-neutral or reduced-impact claims based on offsetting, no. 2a self-made sustainability labels (including social ones), no. 10a presenting a legal duty such as the ESPR donation offer as a distinctive feature; sec. 5(3) no. 4 UWG on future claims without a verifiable plan. The blacklist applies to consumer-facing practice, but public channels reach consumers and sec. 5(1) UWG applies to all; BGH I ZR 98/23 (27 June 2024, Katjes) required that an ambiguous term like "klimaneutral" be explained in the advertisement itself, and that case concerned a trade-press advertisement. Specific, quantified, substantiated statements remain lawful; avoided emissions must be labelled with method, factor and date and reported outside the company inventory, never converted into a neutrality claim. Enforcement is private: competitors and qualified associations under sec. 8(3) UWG, warning-letter costs under sec. 13 UWG; fines under sec. 19 UWG only in coordinated EU actions. [IT refresh: donate, sell or recycle](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/it-refresh-spenden-verkaufen-itad.html): decision guide for the old fleet at a hardware refresh, written per lot rather than per fleet. Three routes: sale (remarketing, buy-back, lease return) realises residual value and yields an invoice but no nameable recipient; donation to a tax-exempt body may be withdrawn at book value under sec. 6(1) no. 4 sentence 4 EStG, so no gain arises, but the deductible amount is then only that withdrawal value plus the VAT on the withdrawal (sec. 10b(3) sentence 2 EStG; sec. 9(2) sentence 3 KStG), which is small for depreciated devices; recovery makes the device waste and triggers ElektroG duties (manufacturer take-back option for non-household equipment, sec. 19(1) ElektroG). VAT on the donation is a deemed supply under sec. 3(1b) sentence 1 no. 3 UStG measured by the notional purchase price at the time of donation (sec. 10(4) sentence 1 no. 1 UStG; BMF circular of 18 March 2021, UStAE 10.6(1a)), i.e. second-hand value, not list price. A working device sold or donated is not waste (sec. 3(1) sentence 1 KrWG) but reuse of a non-waste product (sec. 3(21) KrWG), ranked above recycling in the hierarchy of sec. 6(1) KrWG. Data erasure under Art. 32 GDPR is a constant across all three routes. The guide states openly that for young devices with market value selling is usually the better deal and that the case for donating is the documented recipient and the reuse data for ESRS E5 / VSME B7 reporting, not the tax effect. Includes a per-lot decision matrix (market value, condition, evidence need, timing, volume) and a rollout timeline from T-8 weeks, and cites the Bitkom survey of February 2026 (74 per cent of companies 'properly dispose of' still-functional devices, 33 per cent donate, 12 per cent sell to refurbishers). English version: [IT refresh: donate, sell or recycle](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/it-refresh-donate-sell-recycle.html) (EU-wide: Art. 16 and 74 VAT Directive 2006/112/EC, Art. 3(1), 3(13), 4(1) Waste Framework Directive 2008/98/EC, Art. 13(1) WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU, Art. 32 GDPR). [Office move: handing back the premises](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/bueroumzug-mietflaeche-rueckgabe-sachspende.html) (German; English version at https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/office-move-lease-handover-donation.html): the lease end date sets the pace of any move. Under German law the tenant must return the premises when the lease ends (sec. 546(1) BGB); if they are withheld, the landlord may claim compensation at the agreed or local market rent for the period of withholding, and further damages are not excluded (sec. 546a BGB). Tenant fixtures may be removed (sec. 539(2) BGB); whether they must be, and to what condition the premises are returned, is a matter for the lease. The guide sorts the inventory into four piles (move, sell, donate, dispose) in the order of the waste hierarchy (sec. 6(1) KrWG), explains why donations need the longest lead time (need, space and transport must coincide at the recipient) and gives a backwards plan from T-12 weeks with one rule for the final weeks: recipients first, then buyers, then the skip. Leased equipment goes back to the lessor and cannot be donated. [Store closure: donating the shop fittings](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/filialschliessung-ladeneinrichtung-spenden.html) (German; English version at https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/store-closure-shop-fittings-donation.html): separates the stock (goods for resale, VAT under sec. 3(1b) and 10(4) UStG, EU destruction ban under Art. 25 Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 for apparel and footwear) from the shop fittings (business equipment, book-value election under sec. 6(1) no. 4 sentence 4 EStG). Lists which fittings non-profits can use (system shelving, clothes rails, plug-in refrigeration; bespoke counters only rarely). A till is an electronic recording system: its decommissioning must be notified to the tax office within one month (sec. 146a(4) AO) and its data secured for the retention period (sec. 147 AO) before any device is wiped. Refrigeration on a central plant requires recovery of fluorinated gases before decommissioning by certified personnel (Art. 8(1), 8(2) and 10 Regulation (EU) 2024/573) and is rarely suitable as a donation. In insolvency the power of disposal passes to the administrator (sec. 80(1) InsO), who must realise the estate (sec. 159 InsO); donating fittings that would otherwise cost the estate to strip out needs the administrator's consent. [Returns and overstock: donate instead of destroy](https://surpluspurpose.com/guides/returns-overstock-donate-instead-of-destroy.html) (English, EU-wide; German version at https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/retouren-ueberbestaende-spenden-statt-vernichten.html): the destruction ban of Art. 25 Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 for clothing, accessories, headgear and footwear (large companies since 19 July 2026, medium-sized from 19 July 2030), the donation-offer derogation in Art. 2(h) Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/296 (at least three suitable social economy entities in the Union or the company website, at least eight weeks, five-year records produced within 30 days), the broader Art. 24 disclosure duty, VAT on donated returns under Art. 16 and 74 of the VAT Directive valued by condition at the time of donation, a comparison of stock buyer, outlet, donation and destruction, and how an online shop plugs donation into returns grading: a rule for items of limited marketability, one collection point per site, a weekly file with product group, quantity, condition class, weight and location, and the handover confirmation fed back into inventory management. [Liability for in-kind donations, German](https://surpluspurpose.com/de/ratgeber/haftung-sachspende-unternehmen.html): what a donating company is liable for and what it is not, in five layers. Contract: a donation is a gift, so the donor is liable only for intent and gross negligence (sec. 521 BGB) and for defects only if fraudulently concealed (sec. 524(1) BGB; legal defects sec. 523 BGB); liability for intent cannot be waived in advance (sec. 276(3) BGB) and standard terms cannot exclude gross negligence or personal injury (sec. 309 no. 7 BGB), so the goal is not "no liability" but "no liability event". Product safety: Regulation (EU) 2023/988 (GPSR) covers free-of-charge supply in the course of a business (Art. 3(6)) and expressly used products (Art. 2(3)), but only products intended for or likely to be used by consumers (Art. 3(1)); the donor is a distributor with due-diligence duties under Art. 12; products that must be repaired before use are out of scope if clearly labelled (Art. 2(3) sentence 2). Product liability: strict liability falls on the manufacturer (sec. 1, 4(1)-(2) ProdHaftG); a supplier is treated as manufacturer only if it cannot name the manufacturer within one month (sec. 4(3) ProdHaftG), which the handover record with manufacturer, model and serial number answers; Directive (EU) 2024/2853 applies to products placed on the market from 9 December 2026. Transport: risk passes on handover (sec. 446, 447 BGB by analogy); a carrier is liable between takeover and delivery (sec. 425 HGB) up to 8.33 SDR per kilogram (sec. 431 HGB), the sender must load and pack safely for carriage (sec. 412 HGB); damaged lithium batteries may not travel (ADR special provision 188). Data, licences, tax: erasure is processing (Art. 4(2) GDPR), accountability Art. 5(2), processor contract Art. 28; software without a transferable licence breaches sec. 69c no. 3 UrhG; the donation receipt is issued by the recipient, who bears the 30 per cent issuer liability (sec. 10b(4) sentences 2-3 EStG), while the donor risks only loss of the deduction (sentence 1). Five product groups with the decisive norm each (office furniture; IT; tools and machinery - used machines already placed on the EEA market are not newly placed on the market, Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 applies from 20 January 2027; textiles - separate collection of waste textiles since 1 January 2025 under sec. 20(2) sentence 1 no. 6 KrWG, PPE under Regulation (EU) 2016/425; materials such as single-polymer plastic film - product rather than waste only if a new use follows immediately under sec. 3(3) sentence 1 no. 2 KrWG, food contact only with a declaration of conformity under Art. 16 Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004). Worked example: a Munich IT consultancy donating 238 devices to 16 non-profits with per-device manufacturer, model, serial number and condition class A-E. Five handover-record fields that close every layer: identity, condition, safety, data and licence, handover.

## How it works
Corporates list non-perishable, reusable surplus in good condition. sur.plus matches it with verified NGOs and coordinates logistics and cross-border customs documentation. Every match produces a CSRD-ready impact report and a pre-filled donation certificate (Spendenbescheinigung). Excluded for safety and compliance: food and drink, pharmaceuticals and medical devices, hazardous materials, weapons and controlled goods.

## For whom
- Corporates: turn disposal costs and idle surplus into documented social impact and tax-deductible in-kind donations (Sachspende).
- NGOs: receive needed goods, free of charge.

## Public goal
500 verified NGOs in the network by the end of 2027 (17 as of August 2026), visualised on the homepage as a field of 500 door-lights. "NGO" here means any organisation that can lawfully receive an in-kind donation: tax-privileged charitable organisations (e.V., gGmbH, gUG, charitable foundations and cooperatives) and public institutions (schools, kindergartens, municipal bodies, churches). Only organisations that have passed sur.plus verification are counted.

## Pricing
- Clearance & Logistics - one-off project, fixed price quoted before we start: pickup and packing via vetted logistics partners, certified data erasure with per-device certificates, refurbishment and re-use via social service partners, interim storage, distribution across multiple NGOs, donation certificates prepared by sur.plus as far as possible and released and countersigned by the receiving NGOs, and one reporting-ready impact report. No subscription required. Covers operating assets and materials (IT, furniture, tools, building materials) and, since the ESPR destruction ban, unsold clothing, clothing accessories, headgear and footwear - including the documented eight-week donation offer to at least three social economy entities in the EU that Art. 2(h) of Delegated Reg. (EU) 2026/296 requires. Not for food. Unsold goods that remain saleable are a deemed supply for VAT under sec. 3(1b) UStG, assessed at replacement cost under sec. 10(4) UStG; the zero valuation in the BMF letter of 18 March 2021 applies only to goods of limited marketability.
- Pulse - €0: surplus assessment only, no account needed (leads into free registration)
- Registration - €0: browse open needs from verified NGOs, anonymised (category, focus, region). NGO identity, contact, coordinated matching and CSRD documentation require Seed or Tree.
- Seed - €990/year (effectively €83/month), or €99/month billed monthly: up to 12 matches per year, unused matches roll over (up to 6), 2 seats, AI Copilot (listings, impact copy, match scoring, social-media impact cards), export in Voluntary Standard format, evidence pack for the ESPR donation offer, vetted logistics partners ready to book, coordinated pickup on request (transport billed at cost), access to the social service partner network, weekly impact & NGO-needs newsletter, marketing dashboard
- Tree - €3,890/year (effectively €324/month), or €389/month billed monthly: everything in Seed plus unlimited matches, curated priority matching, CSRD documentation per match with method and date per figure and a complete audit trail, donation certificate per match as tax-relevant evidence, 5 seats, priority support
- Scale & Enterprise - individual pricing: for organisations with more than 500 employees, multiple sites or recurring returns and overstock lots, quoted on request
- NGOs: free of charge

## Methodology
- Carbon: GHG Protocol (avoided emissions, reported separately from SBTi inventory reductions)
- Social value: GIIN IRIS+
- Reporting: ESRS (focus E5 resource use & circular economy, E1 climate, S3 affected communities) / CSRD / Voluntary Standard (the VSME successor, adopted 3 July 2026, not yet in the Official Journal)
- Frameworks: SDGs (esp. 12 & 13), EU waste hierarchy / R-strategies (reuse-first, R3/R7)
- Regulatory drivers: CSRD post-Omnibus; Voluntary Standard value chain cap (binding via Directive (EU) 2026/470, covering companies up to 1,000 employees, no assurance required); ESPR ban on destruction of unsold goods (large companies since 19 July 2026, medium-sized from 19 July 2030) and the Article 24 annual disclosure of discarded unsold consumer goods across all product categories
